newsitem.title: INDONESIA: New Indonesia human rights chief wins acceptance.
newsitem.headline: New Indonesia human rights chief wins acceptance.

text.p: The new chairman of Indonesia's official human rights watchdog was unlikely to lead any confrontation with the government, lawyers and diplomats said on Wednesday.
But the chairman, a former religious affairs minister and current adviser to President Suharto, was expected to keep the body independent and maintain its hard-won integrity, they said.
The high-profile National Commission on Human Rights, set up by the government in 1993, elected Munawir Sjadzali as its chairman at a meeting on Tuesday night.
Lawyers and diplomats said they did not anticipate any change in direction in the organisation following the election of Sjadzali, who is also a former ambassador.

Under its first chairman, former Supreme Court Chief Justice Ali Said, who died in June, the organisation won a reputation for integrity and a willingness to criticise the country's powerful military establishment.

The commission's preliminary report on the July 27 riots that rocked Jakarta caught the government off balance. The report said at least five people died and 74 were missing, while the government gave a figure of four dead and none missing. "The government wants the rights commission to prove the figures with acceptable evidence," State Secretary Murdiono said. The final report is expected to be released shortly.

Sjadzali, currently a member of President Suharto's Supreme Advisory Council, was elected chairman by 19 of the 21 commission members in a 12-7 vote, defeating a member of parliament of Indonesia's ruling Golkar party, Arnold Baramuli.

"It really continues the tradition that was established with Ali Said of picking a trusted insider, but someone who has broader respect and integrity," said a Western diplomat who follows human rights issues.
"They have resisted the temptation to go for someone more flamboyant and less predictable," he said, adding that Sjadzali -- a member of the commission since it was formed -- was a good compromise.
"Picking an ex-diplomat makes sense as the commission has a big role in interpreting for the outside world Indonesia's human rights record and practices," the diplomat said.
Sjadzali, 71, told reporters after his election that he did not have a specific agenda for the commission.
"I do not want to talk too soon about a programme for the commission. I have only just been elected," he said.
Deputy Chairman Marzuki Darusman, who declined to be nominated for the top post, praised Sjadzali's election.
"He is independent, he has integrity and vision," he said.
Indonesian human rights lawyer Mulya Lubis described Sjadzali as a "nice man" who had good access to the government but was an unknown quantity in the field of human rights.

Lubis, who is chairman of the Manila-based Regional Council of Human Rights in Asia, told Reuters that Sjadzali needed to strengthen the body's independence and fact-finding ability in probing rights abuses.
